In theory we say that a quantity is conserved when the amount of it in the world is the same at any one time as at any other. But in practice we cannot survey the whole world, so we have to mean something more manageable. We mean that, taking any given region, if the amount of the quantity in the region has changed, it is because some of the quantity has passed across the boundary of the region. We could even say it would be described in terms of the sense-data of just one person, because we cannot know ohter people's sense-data without some amount of inference. But for now this must stay an ideal. We can get close to it. But if we ever reach it, it will only be after a long period of early work. And we can only see the quite start of that work so far. Still, the inferences we cannot avoid can be guided by certain rules. First, they should always be stated fully and clearly, and in the most general way possible. Second, the things we infer should, whenever possible, be similar to the things whose existence is given to us, intsead of being like Kantian Ding an sich, something completely far from the data that supposedly support the inference. We will allow two kinds of inferred things:, a, other people's sense-data, which are supported by testimony, and which in the end rest on the analogical argument for minds other than our own. B, "sensibilia," which would appear from places wehre there happen to be no minds. And which we assume are real even though they are no one's data. Of these two kinds of ifnerred things, the first will probably be accepted without objection. It would make us happiest if we could do without it and base physics on solipsism. But tohse people, and I'm afraid they are the majority, whose human feelings are stronger than their wish for logical simplicity will surely not share our wish to maek solipsism scientifically acceptable. The second kind of inferred things raises much more serious problems. Some may think it absurd to say that a thing can show any appearance at all in a place where there are no sense organs or nervous structures for it to appear through. We ourselves do not feel this absurdity. Still, we should treat these supposed appearances only as a temporary support, to be used while the building of physics is going up, though it mgiht be possible to remove it once the building is finished. So these "sensibilia," which are not anyone's data, should be taken more as an illustrative hypothesis and help for early statements than as a firm part of the final philosophy of physics.
output: A complete application of the method which substitutes constructions for inferences would exhibit matter wholly in terms of sense-data, and even, we may add, of the sense-data of a single person, since the sense-data of others cannot be known without some element of inference. This, however, must remain for the present an ideal, to be approached as nearly as possible, but to be reached, if at all, only after a long preliminary labour of which as yet we can only see the very beginning. The inferences which are unavoidable can, however, be subjected to certain guiding principles. In the first place they should always be made perfectly explicit, and should be formulated in the most general manner possible. In the second place the inferred entities should, whenever this can be done, be similar to those whose existence is given, rather than, like the Kantian Ding an sich, something wholly remote from the data which nominally support the inference. The inferred entities which we shall allow ourselves are of two kinds: (a) the sense-data of other people, in favour of which there is the evidence of testimony, resting ultimately upon the analogical argument in favour of minds other than our own; (b) the "sensibilia" which would appear from places where there happen to be no minds, and which we suppose to be real although they are no one's data.
